docs.title: Experimental Validation of Control Methods
docs.text:
Welcome to the supplementary website accompanying my research internship thesis: Data-driven Optimal Control on Quanser Qube.

Author: Jort Stammen Supervisors: Sasha Pogromskiy (TU/e), Dragan Nesic (UoM), Mathieu Granzotto (UoM) Institutions: Eindhoven University of Technology (TU/e) & The University of Melbourne (UoM)

docs.title: About This Website
docs.text:
This website presents synchronized animations, video recordings, and key metrics from the experimental evaluation of model-based and data-driven control methods on physical hardware. Because closed-loop dynamics—such as disturbance recovery, limit cycles, and servo drift—cannot be fully captured on paper, this platform provides a visual complement to the thesis.

Figure: The Quanser QUBE-Servo 2 experimental setup used for all validations.

docs.title: The Experiments
docs.text: The experiments are organized following the structure of the thesis and demonstrate discounted Linear Quadratic Regulation (LQR) on the Quanser QUBE-Servo 2 in both its inertia-disc and rotary inverted-pendulum configurations.

docs.title: Model-Based Methods (Chapter 2 & 5)
docs.text:
Experimental validation of model-based stabilizing near-optimal controllers synthesised from the linearised upright pendulum model.

  • Baseline Controllers: Comparison of convex LMI designs (\(\hat{K}_\gamma\) and \(\bar{K}_\gamma\)) and stabilizing policy iteration (sPI) at \(\gamma = 0.5\), \(\alpha = 0.98\).
  • \(\alpha\)- and \(\gamma\)-Sweeps: Manual-push robustness and steady-state tests mapping the usable operating window under servo drift and \(\pm 10\text{ V}\) actuator saturation.

Explore Model-Based Experiments

docs.title: Data-Driven Methods (Chapter 3 & 5)
docs.text:
Experimental validation of direct (noise-free and noisy LMI) and indirect (least-squares and instrumental-variable) controllers synthesised from measured input–state data.

  • Inertia Disc: Open-loop excitation and closed-loop reference tracking (\(5^\circ\) and \(50^\circ\) square waves, chirp).
  • Pendulum Balance Control: Closed-loop probing and programmed-pulse disturbance rejection, comparing direct, indirect, and relaxed noisy LMI designs.

Explore Data-Driven Experiments

docs.title: How to Use This Website
docs.text:
Select an experiment from the navigation menu to find:

  1. Setup & Parameters: The controller parameters (e.g., \(\gamma\), \(\alpha\), \(T_s\)) and synthesised gains.
  2. Synchronized Videos: Side-by-side MATLAB logged responses and physical hardware recordings.
  3. Observations: Key experimental takeaways, including recovery, saturation, and steady-state behaviour.

docs.title: Relation to the Thesis
docs.text: All experiments correspond directly to Chapter 5 (Experimental Results) of the thesis. The theoretical foundations are presented in Chapter 2 (Model-Based) and Chapter 3 (Data-Driven), while the hardware platform and real-time implementation are detailed in Chapter 4.

docs.title: Data-Driven Experiments
docs.text: This section presents the experimental validation of the data-driven discounted LQR designs on the Quanser QUBE-Servo 2 (Section 5.2). Using offline input–state trajectories collected directly from hardware, the experiments compare direct noise-free (Theorem 3.13), direct noisy (original Theorem 3.19 and relaxed Theorem 3.20), and indirect certainty-equivalence synthesis (least squares and instrumental variables followed by Theorem 2.9) across two progressively more demanding configurations.

docs.title: 1. Inertia Disc (Open-Loop Data & Reference Tracking)
docs.text:
With the pendulum replaced by a rotary inertia disc (\(n = 3\), \(m = 1\)), the QUBE is open-loop marginally stable, enabling exogenous open-loop excitation without feedback correlation. Controllers are synthesised at \(\gamma = 0.9048\) (\(\tau_\gamma = 0.1\text{ s}\)) and \(\alpha = 0.9802\) (\(\tau_\alpha = 0.5\text{ s}\)) from \(T = 1000\) transitions under a period-mismatched \(3\text{ V}\) PRBS (D1) and a clean \(8\text{ V}\) multisine (D2), then validated in closed-loop tracking across \(5^\circ\) and \(50^\circ\) square waves and a \(0.005\text{-}0.5\text{ Hz}\) chirp.

View Inertia-Disc Experiments

docs.title: 2. Inverted Pendulum (Closed-Loop Probing & Balance Control)
docs.text:
With the pendulum module attached (\(n = 4\), \(m = 1\)), the upright equilibrium is open-loop unstable (\(+13.36\text{ rad/s}\) pole), requiring closed-loop probing around \(K_{\text{st}} = \hat{K}_\gamma\) at the destabilising discount factor \(\gamma = 0.5\) (\(\rho(A + BK_\gamma^\star) \approx 1.11\)) and \(\alpha = 0.98\). Controllers synthesised from \(T \approx 2000\) transitions under a \(0.8\text{ V}\) multisine (P1) and a \(0.5\text{ V}\) PRBS (P2) are validated under repeatable \(1.80\text{ V}\) voltage-pulse disturbances—highlighting direct–indirect coincidence on clean data, closed-loop LS bias vs. IV consistency, relaxed vs. original noisy LMI conservatism, and the \(K_\psi \gtrsim 0.9\text{ V/rad}\) drift threshold.

View Pendulum Experiments

docs.title: Experimental setup
docs.text:
For the open-loop data-driven experiments, the pendulum module on the Quanser QUBE-Servo 2 is replaced by a rotary inertia disc. A brushed DC motor drives the disc in the horizontal plane via a single voltage input \(u = V_m\) (\(\pm 10\text{ V}\) operating range), while the yaw angle \(\psi\) is measured by an optical incremental encoder (\(2048\text{ counts/rev}\), \(0.176^\circ\) resolution) and the yaw rate \(\dot{\psi}\) is obtained from a digital tachometer.

Because servo position acts as a pure integrator, the inertia disc is open-loop marginally stable, allowing exogenous open-loop excitation without feedback correlation in least squares. To formulate reference tracking (\(\psi_k \to r_k\)) as regulation to the origin, the state is augmented with an exact tracking-error integrator:

\[ v_{k+1} = v_k + T_s(\psi_k - r_k), \qquad \bar{x}_k = \begin{bmatrix} \psi_k \\ \dot{\psi}_k \\ v_k \end{bmatrix}, \qquad u_k = K \bar{x}_k. \]

All six controllers are synthesised from \(T = 1000\) transitions (averaged from four \(10\text{ s}\) periods at \(T_s = 10\text{ ms}\)) collected under two excitation signals:

  • D1 (PRBS \(3\text{ V}\)): Period-mismatched averaging stress test (\(5.22\%\) LS residual, \(\hat{\eta} = 7.90 \times 10^{-3}\)).
  • D2 (Multisine \(8\text{ V}\)): Clean odd-harmonic baseline (\(1.04\%\) LS residual, \(\hat{\eta} = 3.67 \times 10^{-4}\)).

docs.title: Reference Tracking Experiments
docs.text: All six controllers are tested on hardware across three trajectories:

docs.title: 1. \(5^\circ\) Square Wave (\(0.125\text{ Hz}\))
docs.text:
Investigates small-signal static friction (\(\approx 0.18\text{--}0.20\text{ V}\)), integrator wind-up delay after reversals, and steady-state error.

View \(5^\circ\) Square Wave Experiments

docs.title: 2. \(50^\circ\) Square Wave (\(0.125\text{ Hz}\))
docs.text:
Investigates large-signal slewing speed, overshoot, settling time, and the experimental coincidence between direct noise-free and indirect (LS) synthesis on clean data (Proposition 3.30).

View \(50^\circ\) Square Wave Experiments

docs.title: 3. \(0.005\text{--}0.5\text{ Hz}\) Chirp (\(10\text{ s}\) period)
docs.text:
Investigates dynamic frequency-response tracking, phase lag without feedforward, and control effort across increasing frequencies.

View Chirp Experiments

docs.title: Inertia Disc: \(0.005\text{-}0.5\text{ Hz}\) Chirp Tracking
docs.text: All six controllers (D1 and D2 × Direct noise-free, Direct noisy, and Indirect LS) are tested on a \(0.005\text{--}0.5\text{ Hz}\) chirp reference (\(10\text{ s}\) period, \(0\%\) saturation).

docs.title: Observations
docs.text:
• Without feedforward, all five well-posed designs exhibit phase lag (\(\text{nRMSE} \in [73.9\%, 94.6\%]\), \(\text{RMS } u \approx 0.21\text{ V}\), \(\max|u| \le 0.41\text{ V}\)).
  • D2 Direct, noisy achieves the lowest tracking error (\(\text{RMSE} = 74.0^\circ\), \(\text{nRMSE} = 73.9\%\)), while D2 Direct, noise-free and D2 Indirect (LS) remain identical (\(\text{RMSE} = 85.3^\circ\)).
  • D1 Direct, noisy barely tracks the chirp (\(\text{nRMSE} = 101.3\%\), \(\text{RMS } u = 0.54\text{ V}\), \(\max|u| = 1.36\text{ V}\)).

docs.text: All six controllers (D1 and D2 × Direct noise-free, Direct noisy, and Indirect LS) are tested on a \(5^\circ\) square wave at \(0.125\text{ Hz}\) (\(24\text{ s}\), metrics averaged over five full swings).

docs.title: Observations
docs.text:
• Overcoming static friction (\(\approx 0.18\text{-}0.20\text{ V}\)) causes an integrator wind-up delay after reversals.
  • D2 Direct, noisy (\(K_v = -1.9331\)) breaks stiction fastest (\(\approx 1\text{ s}\)) and is the only controller to settle within \(2\%\) (\(t_s = 2.74\text{ s}\), \(e_{\text{ss}} = 0.14^\circ\)).
  • D2 Direct, noise-free and D2 Indirect (LS) wait \(\approx 2\text{ s}\) and produce virtually identical responses (\(e_{\text{ss}} \approx 0.45^\circ\)).
  • D1 Direct, noise-free and D1 Indirect (LS) stall near \(0^\circ\) (\(e_{\text{ss}} \approx 5.4^\circ\)), while D1 Direct, noisy (\(\max|u| = 0.065\text{ V}\)) never breaks stiction (\(\psi \equiv 0^\circ\)).

docs.title: Experimental setup
docs.text:
For the closed-loop data-driven balance experiments, the pendulum module is attached to the Quanser QUBE-Servo 2. A brushed DC motor drives the rotary arm (\(\psi\)) in the horizontal plane via a single voltage input \(u = V_m\) (\(\pm 10\text{ V}\) operating range), while the pendulum swings freely about the arm (\(\phi\)). Both angles are measured by optical incremental encoders (\(2048\text{ counts/rev}\), \(0.176^\circ\) resolution). Servo yaw rate \(\dot{\psi}\) is obtained from a digital tachometer, and the upright pendulum velocity \(\dot{\delta\phi}\) is estimated via the filtered derivative \(H(s) = \frac{s}{(1/50)s + 1}\) at \(T_s = 10\text{ ms}\).

In the upright equilibrium (\(\delta\phi = \phi - \pi = 0\)), the pendulum is open-loop unstable (\(+13.36\text{ rad/s}\) pole, \(z \approx 1.143\) at \(T_s = 10\text{ ms}\)). Data are therefore collected in closed loop by adding an exogenous probing signal \(e_k\) to the model-based baseline controller \(K_{\text{st}} = \hat{K}_\gamma\):

\[ u_k = K_{\text{st}} \xi_k + e_k, \qquad x_k = \begin{bmatrix} \delta\phi_k \\ \psi_k \\ \dot{\delta\phi}_k \\ \dot{\psi}_k \end{bmatrix}. \]

After manual upright engagement before \(t = 10\text{ s}\), \(e_k\) is applied for \(20\text{ s}\) of a \(30\text{ s}\) run, yielding \(T \approx 2000\) transitions per record. From an excitation amplitude sweep, two datasets inside the linear regime (\(|\delta\phi| \lesssim 10^\circ\)) are selected for controller synthesis:

  • P1 (Multisine \(0.8\text{ V}\)): Odd-harmonic multisine (\(\text{RMS}(e)/\text{RMS}(u) \approx 52\%\), \(\kappa(\Omega) = 6.31\), \(10.3\%\) LS residual, \(\hat{\eta} = 0.11\), \(\max|\delta\phi| = 7.38^\circ\)).
  • P2 (PRBS \(0.5\text{ V}\)): Binary excitation (\(\text{RMS}(e)/\text{RMS}(u) \approx 65\%\), \(\kappa(\Omega) = 6.56\), \(7.7\%\) LS residual, \(\hat{\eta} = 0.053\)).

  • Guaranteed Decay Rate (\(\alpha\)): \(0.98\)
  • Costs & Noisy Margin: \(Q = \text{diag}(100, 30, 10, 1)\), \(R = 10\), \(\mu_{\text{frac}} = 0.5\)

docs.title: 1. Closed-Loop Probing Signals (Data Collection)
docs.text:
Demonstrates the \(30\text{ s}\) closed-loop excitation protocol around \(K_{\text{st}} = \hat{K}_\gamma\) for both selected probing signals (P1: Multisine \(0.8\text{ V}\) and P2: PRBS \(0.5\text{ V}\)), illustrating the trade-off between persistence of excitation and keeping pendulum excursions within the \(\sim 10^\circ\) linear regime.

View Probing Signal Experiments

docs.title: 2. Programmed-Pulse Robustness Tests
docs.text:
Evaluates key synthesised controllers under repeatable \(1.80\text{ V}\) voltage pulse disturbances (\(40\text{ s}\) runs, pulses at \(t \in \{13, 17, 21, 25, 29, 33\}\text{ s}\)), highlighting direct vs. indirect performance against \(\hat{K}_\gamma\), closed-loop LS bias, original vs. relaxed noisy LMI conservatism, and the \(K_\psi \gtrsim 0.9\text{ V/rad}\) drift threshold.

View Robustness Test Experiments

docs.title: Pendulum: Closed-Loop Probing Signals
docs.text: Because the inverted pendulum is open-loop unstable (\(+13.36\text{ rad/s}\) pole), excitation data must be collected in closed loop using \(u_k = K_{\text{st}}\xi_k + e_k\) with \(K_{\text{st}} = \hat{K}_\gamma\). After manual upright engagement prior to \(t = 10\text{ s}\), the probing signal \(e_k\) is injected for \(20\text{ s}\) of a \(30\text{ s}\) run (\(T \approx 2000\) transitions at \(T_s = 10\text{ ms}\)).

docs.title: Excitation Trade-off & Diagnostics (Table C.7)
docs.text:
• P1 (Multisine \(0.8\text{ V}\)): Odd harmonics (\(0.1\text{-}6\text{ Hz}\), crest factor \(\approx 2.06\)) keep pendulum excursions inside the linear regime (\(\max|\delta\phi| = 7.38^\circ\)), contributing \(\approx 52\%\) of input RMS with a \(10.3\%\) LS residual and \(\hat{\eta} = 0.11\).
  • P2 (PRBS \(0.5\text{ V}\)): Flat-spectrum binary sequence (\(5\text{ Hz}\) clock, crest factor \(= 1\)) achieves a higher probing share (\(\approx 65\%\) of input RMS) and roughly halves both the LS residual (\(7.7\%\)) and noise proxy (\(\hat{\eta} = 0.053\)) while staying well within safety and linear bounds.

docs.title: Pendulum: Programmed-Pulse Robustness Tests
docs.text:
To evaluate disturbance rejection and steady-state servo behaviour under repeatable conditions, the data-driven controllers are tested over \(40\text{ s}\) runs with six pre-programmed \(1.80\text{ V}\) voltage pulses at \(t \in \{13, 17, 21, 25, 29, 33\}\text{ s}\) (signs \(+, -, +, -, -, +\), \(0\%\) saturation across all runs).

The five recordings below capture the representative behaviours highlighted in Section 5.2.4 (Table C.9, benchmark \(\hat{K}_\gamma\) cost \(J = 24.1\)):

  • Best overall data-driven performance: P2 Indirect (IV) cuts empirical disturbance cost by \(16\%\) relative to the analytical model baseline (\(J = 20.4\), \(0.84 \times J_{\hat{K}_\gamma}\)) while matching the imposed decay rate \(\alpha = 0.98\) (\(\hat{\rho} = 0.981\)).
  • Closed-loop LS bias: P1 Indirect (LS) suffers errors-in-variables bias, yielding the worst P1 cost (\(J = 40.2\), \(1.67 \times J_{\hat{K}_\gamma}\)), largest peak pendulum error (\(8.08^\circ\)), and a \(2.65^\circ\) quiet limit cycle.
  • Direct noise-free vs. analytical baseline: P1 Direct, noise-free achieves the smallest servo swing across all designs (\(\max|\psi| = 19.8^\circ\)) and outperforms \(\hat{K}_\gamma\) in cost (\(J = 21.5\), \(0.89 \times J_{\hat{K}_\gamma}\)).
  • Original vs. relaxed noisy LMIs & the \(K_\psi \gtrsim 0.9\text{ V/rad}\) threshold: On P2, Direct, noisy (original) (\(K_\psi = 0.677\text{ V/rad}\)) drifts into the \(130^\circ\) safety cut-off at \(t = 9.7\text{ s}\) before the first pulse, whereas Direct, noisy (relaxed) (\(K_\psi = 0.708\text{ V/rad}\)) survives all pulses at the cost of large servo swings (\(\max|\psi| = 61.1^\circ\), \(J = 75.7\)).

Lowest disturbance cost overall (\(J = 20.4\), \(0.84 \times J_{\hat{K}_\gamma}\)), \(\max|\delta\phi| = 5.82^\circ\), \(\max|\psi| = 23.1^\circ\), \(\hat{\rho} = 0.981\).

docs.title: Model-Based Controller Experiments
docs.text: This section presents the experimental validation of the model-based discounted LQR designs on the Quanser QUBE-Servo 2 rotary inverted pendulum (Section 5.1). Using the fourth-order reduced linearised upright model (\(n = 4\), \(m = 1\), \(T_s = 10\text{ ms}\), \(Q = \text{diag}(100, 30, 10, 1)\), \(R = 10\)) at the destabilising discount factor \(\gamma = 0.5\) (\(\rho(A + BK_\gamma^\star) \approx 1.11\)), the experiments evaluate the guaranteed-cost LMI (\(\hat{K}_\gamma\), Theorem 2.9), the guaranteed-gain-error LMI (\(\bar{K}_\gamma\), Theorem 2.12), and stabilizing policy iteration (sPI, Algorithm 1)—progressing from nominal baseline tests to parameter sweeps that map the physical operating limits of the hardware.

docs.title: 1. Baseline Controllers (\(\gamma = 0.5\), \(\alpha = 0.98\))
docs.text:
Evaluates all four baseline designs (\(\hat{K}_\gamma\), \(\bar{K}_\gamma\), and their sPI refinements) on hardware under manual pushes and steady-state balancing. Although \(\bar{K}_\gamma\) and its sPI refinement achieve lower model cost, their weak servo feedback (\(K_\psi \approx 0.47\text{ V/rad}\)) fails to overcome unmodelled Coulomb stiction and encoder-cable asymmetry, causing monotonic servo drift into the \(130^\circ\) safety cut-off—whereas \(\hat{K}_\gamma\) (\(K_\psi = 0.98\text{ V/rad}\)) and its sPI refinement balance and recover with empirical decay factors \(\hat{\rho} \approx \alpha\).

View Baseline Controller Experiments

docs.title: 2. Decay Rate (\(\alpha\)) Sweep (\(\gamma = 0.5\), \(\alpha \in [0.94, 0.99]\))
docs.text:
Sweeps the prescribed decay rate \(\alpha\) from \(0.99\) down to \(0.94\) using manual-push robustness and \(30\text{ s}\) steady-state tests to isolate the hardware operating window, revealing three regimes:

  1. Large \(\alpha\) (\(\ge 0.98\)): The pendulum balances, but weak servo feedback (\(K_\psi < 0.9\text{ V/rad}\)) permits slow servo wander and drift in \(\bar{K}_\gamma\) (settling requires \(\alpha \le 0.97\) for \(\bar{K}_\gamma\) and \(\alpha \le 0.98\) for \(\hat{K}_\gamma\)).
  2. Usable window (\(\alpha_{\text{conv}} \in \{0.965, 0.97\}\)): Both \(\hat{K}_\gamma\) and \(\bar{K}_\gamma\) settle the servo and reject disturbances cleanly without actuator clipping.
  3. Small \(\alpha\) (\(\le 0.96\)): Aggressive pendulum gains (\(|K_\phi| \approx 24\text{ V/rad}\)) trigger \(\pm 10\text{ V}\) saturation during pushes, inducing sustained limit-cycle oscillations (with calibration failing at \(\alpha = 0.94\)).

This archive features representative robustness runs at \(\alpha \in \{0.97, 0.965\}\) for \(\bar{K}_\gamma\) and \(\alpha \in \{0.965, 0.96, 0.94\}\) for \(\hat{K}_\gamma\).

View \(\alpha\)-Sweep Experiments

docs.title: 3. Discount Factor (\(\gamma\)) Sweep (\(\alpha = 0.97\), \(\gamma \in \{0.2, 0.5, 0.8, 0.9\}\))
docs.text:
Fixes \(\alpha = 0.97\) inside the common usable window and varies \(\gamma \in \{0.2, 0.5, 0.8, 0.9\}\) to isolate the effect of discounting on hardware behaviour. Because \(\gamma\) enters Theorem 2.9 directly via \(\sqrt{\gamma}A_d\) and \(\sqrt{\gamma}B_d\), \(\hat{K}_\gamma\) scales strongly with \(\gamma\) and saturates the \(\pm 10\text{ V}\) limit during pushes for \(\gamma \ge 0.8\) (\(|\hat{K}_\phi| \ge 23.7\text{ V/rad}\)); by contrast, boundary-pinned \(\bar{K}_\gamma\) varies weakly and recovers across all \(\gamma\) (wandering only in steady state at \(\gamma = 0.9\), where \(\bar{K}_\psi = 0.75\text{ V/rad} < 0.9\text{ V/rad}\)).

View \(\gamma\)-Sweep Experiments

docs.title: Model-Based Decay-Rate (\(\alpha\)) Sweep
docs.text:
In the baseline experiments (\(\alpha = 0.98\), \(\gamma = 0.5\)), the guaranteed-cost controller (\(\hat{K}_\gamma\)) successfully balanced the pendulum, whereas the guaranteed gain error controller (\(\bar{K}_\gamma\)) lost the servo to drift despite having a lower theoretical cost and the same nominal decay-rate certificate.

To understand why this happens—and to map the practical operating limits of both designs—the guaranteed decay rate \(\alpha\) is swept while keeping all other baseline parameters fixed. Specifically, this sweep answers four questions:

  1. Does there exist an \(\alpha \in (0, 1)\) for which \(\bar{K}_\gamma\) avoids servo drift?
  2. Does there exist an \(\alpha \in (0, 1)\) for which \(\hat{K}_\gamma\) experiences servo drift?
  3. What is the practical lower limit \(\alpha_{\text{lim}}\) below which actuator saturation (\(\pm 10\text{ V}\)) prevents disturbance recovery?
  4. Is there a common window \(\alpha_{\text{conv}}\) where both designs balance, avoid drift, and avoid saturation?

docs.title: Fixed Parameters
docs.text:
Unless otherwise specified, all controllers in the \(\alpha\)-sweep were synthesized using:

  • Sample Time (\(T_s\)): 10 ms
  • Discount Factor (\(\gamma\)): 0.5 (optimal closed loop is unstable with \(\rho(A + B K^\star_\gamma) \approx 1.11\))
  • State Cost (\(Q\)): \(\text{diag}(100, 30, 10, 1)\)
  • Input Cost (\(R\)): 10
  • Swept Parameter (\(\alpha\)): \([0.80, 1.50]\) (theoretical) and \(0.99 \to 0.94\) (hardware)

docs.title: 1. Hardware Robustness Test: Guaranteed Cost (\(\hat{K}_\gamma\))
docs.text:
The guaranteed-cost controller is tested on the Quanser QUBE-Servo 2 from \(\alpha = 0.99\) down to \(\alpha = 0.94\) under manual impulsive pushes to determine its disturbance-rejection range and saturation limit.

  • Observation: Shows no servo drift across the tested range and recovers cleanly down to \(\alpha = 0.965\) (\(\hat{\alpha}_{\text{lim}} \approx 0.965\)). Below \(\alpha = 0.965\), actuator saturation induces sustained oscillations (\(\alpha = 0.96\)), and by \(\alpha = 0.94\) the controller becomes unstable immediately at calibration.
  • Included Videos: \(\alpha = 0.965\), \(\alpha = 0.96\), and \(\alpha = 0.94\).

View the Guaranteed Cost \(\alpha\)-Sweep Experiments

docs.title: 2. Hardware Robustness Test: Guaranteed Gain Error (\(\bar{K}_\gamma\))
docs.text:
The guaranteed gain error controller is tested over the same \(\alpha \in [0.94, 0.99]\) range to determine whether enforcing a faster decay rate eliminates the servo drift seen in the baseline.

  • Observation: Servo drift disappears once \(\alpha \le 0.975\), and pushes are recovered down to \(\alpha = 0.96\) (\(\bar{\alpha}_{\text{lim}} \approx 0.96\)). Notably, both \(\hat{K}_\gamma\) and \(\bar{K}_\gamma\) lose robustness at the same pendulum-gain threshold (\(|K_\phi| \approx 24\text{ V/rad}\)), even though their nominal \(\alpha\) differs by \(0.01\).
  • Included Videos: \(\alpha = 0.965\) and \(\alpha = 0.96\).

View the Guaranteed Gain Error \(\alpha\)-Sweep Experiments

At each setting, the pendulum is subjected to multiple manual pushes to test disturbance rejection, servo confinement (\(|\psi| < 130^\circ\)), and actuator saturation (\(V_{\text{sat}} = \pm 10\text{ V}\)). This page presents the full sweep summary and the representative experiments at \(\alpha = 0.965\), \(\alpha = 0.96\), and \(\alpha = 0.94\).

This page presents the full sweep summary and the experiments inside the common usable window at \(\alpha = 0.97\) and \(\alpha = 0.965\).

docs.title: Experimental setup
docs.text:
Before performing parameter sweeps over \(\alpha\) and \(\gamma\), the three model-based discounted LQR designs of Chapter 2 are validated on the Quanser QUBE-Servo 2 rotary inverted pendulum (Section 5.1.1–5.1.2). All controllers are synthesised on the fourth-order reduced linearised upright model (\(n = 4\), \(m = 1\), \(T_s = 10\text{ ms}\)) at a destabilising discount factor \(\gamma = 0.5\), where the optimal discounted controller is open-loop/closed-loop unstable (\(\rho(A + BK_\gamma^\star) = 1.1098 > 1\)).

After verifying all theoretical LMI and sPI certificates in simulation (Tables 5.2–5.3), each controller is evaluated on hardware under steady-state balancing and irregular manual pushes. Although \(\bar{K}_\gamma\) and its sPI refinement achieve lower model cost at \(x_0 = [0.1, 0, 0, 0]^\top\), their weak servo feedback (\(K_\psi \approx 0.47\text{ V/rad}\)) fails to overcome unmodelled Coulomb stiction and encoder-cable asymmetry—causing monotonic servo drift into the \(130^\circ\) safety cut-off—whereas \(\hat{K}_\gamma\) (\(K_\psi = 0.98\text{ V/rad}\)) balances and recovers cleanly.

docs.title: 1. Guaranteed Cost Design (\(\hat{K}_\gamma\), Theorem 2.9)
docs.text:
Minimises a convex upper bound \(\text{trace}(\hat{W}_\gamma)\) on the discounted closed-loop cost while enforcing the decay rate \(\alpha = 0.98\) (\(\rho_{\text{model}} = 0.9731\)). Allocates sufficient servo authority (\(K_\psi = 0.9794\text{ V/rad}\)) to balance and recover from all four manual pushes without saturation, settling with a bounded \(\approx 22^\circ\) servo offset.

View Guaranteed Cost Experiment

docs.title: 2. Guaranteed Gain Error Design (\(\bar{K}_\gamma\), Theorem 2.12)
docs.text:
Minimises the spectral-norm distance \(\|\bar{K}_\gamma - K_\gamma^\star\|\) to the unstable optimal gain while enforcing \(\alpha = 0.98\) (\(\rho_{\text{model}} = 0.9799\)). Although it achieves a lower theoretical cost (\(29.14\) vs. \(47.16\)), pushing the closed-loop spectrum onto \(\alpha\) allocates weak servo feedback (\(K_\psi = 0.4684\text{ V/rad}\)), leading to monotonic servo drift into the \(130^\circ\) safety cut-off.

View Guaranteed Gain Error Experiment

docs.title: 3. Stabilizing Policy Iteration (sPI, Algorithm 1)
docs.text:
Iteratively refines both LMI initialisations (\(K_0 = \hat{K}_\gamma\) over \(76\) iterations; \(K_0 = \bar{K}_\gamma\) over \(35\) iterations) via convex combinations with the policy-improvement step under \(\rho(A+BK_j) < \alpha\). Cost drops monotonically (\(27.7\%\) from \(\hat{K}_\gamma\); \(0.39\%\) from \(\bar{K}_\gamma\)), but pushing \(\rho\) onto \(\alpha\) reduces disturbance damping for \(K_0 = \hat{K}_\gamma\) (\(\text{rms}\,\delta_\phi = 1.76^\circ\)) and preserves servo drift for \(K_0 = \bar{K}_\gamma\).

View sPI Controller Experiments

docs.title: Guaranteed Cost Controller (\(\hat{K}_\gamma\))
docs.text:
The guaranteed cost design synthesizes a gain by minimizing an upper bound on the cost of the closed-loop system, while enforcing a strict decay rate of \(\alpha = 0.98\) (with \(\gamma = 0.5\)).

In the hardware tests, this controller successfully balances the pendulum (\(\delta\phi\) converges to zero) and keeps the servo arm relatively stationary, recovering well from manual disturbances.

docs.title: Guaranteed Gain Error Controller (\(\bar{K}_\gamma\))
docs.text:
The guaranteed gain error design aims to find a stabilizing gain that is as close as possible to the optimal (but unstable) discounted gain \(K^\star_\gamma\). We use a baseline decay rate of \(\alpha = 0.98\).

While this controller successfully balances the pendulum, the hardware tests reveal an interesting limitation: the servo arm experiences severe servo drift (wandering). This drift occurs because the controller prioritizes mimicking the optimal gain over stiffening the servo loop, a phenomenon we investigate deeply in the \(\alpha\)-sweep.

docs.text:

docs.title: Stabilizing Policy Iteration (sPI)
docs.text:
The sPI algorithm is an iterative approach that improves a stabilizing gain step-by-step. By taking a convex combination of a standard policy improvement step and the previous gain, it ensures that every iteration remains stabilizing with a prescribed decay rate (\(\alpha = 0.98\)).

The performance of the final sPI controller heavily depends on its initialization (\(K_0\)).

docs.title: Experimental setup
docs.text: Inside the common usable decay-rate window (\(\alpha_{\text{conv}} \in \{0.965, 0.97\}\)), we fix \(\alpha = 0.97\) and vary the discount factor \(\gamma \in \{0.2, 0.5, 0.8, 0.9\}\) with \(Q = \text{diag}(100, 30, 10, 1)\), \(R = 10\), and \(T_s = 10\text{ ms}\). Each controller is evaluated on hardware using the manual-push disturbance-rejection test and a \(30\text{ s}\) disturbance-free steady-state test to determine whether \(\gamma\) visibly alters closed-loop behaviour at fixed \(\alpha\).

docs.title: Asymmetry Between \(\hat{K}_\gamma\) and \(\bar{K}_\gamma\)
docs.text:
• Guaranteed cost (\(\hat{K}_\gamma\)): \(\gamma\) enters the LMIs directly via \(\sqrt{\gamma}A_d\) and \(\sqrt{\gamma}B_d\). Between \(\gamma = 0.2\) and \(\gamma = 0.9\), \(|\hat{K}_\phi|\) increases by \(55\%\) (\(17.2 \to 26.6\text{ V/rad}\)) and \(\hat{K}_\psi\) more than doubles (\(1.22 \to 2.66\text{ V/rad}\)). For \(\gamma \ge 0.8\), \(|\hat{K}_\phi|\) reaches the \(\approx 24\text{ V/rad}\) saturation threshold during pushes, causing \(\pm 10\text{ V}\) clipping and failure to recover.
  • Guaranteed gain error (\(\bar{K}_\gamma\)): \(\gamma\) enters only through the reference \(K_\gamma^\star\). While \(\rho(A_d + B_d K_\gamma^\star) \ge \alpha\), \(\bar{K}_\gamma\) remains pinned to the \(\alpha = 0.97\) boundary (\(\rho_{\text{model}} \approx 0.9700\)) and varies weakly (\(|\bar{K}_\phi| \in [14.7, 17.3]\)), recovering cleanly for all \(\gamma\) (though \(\bar{K}_\psi = 0.75\text{ V/rad} < 0.9\text{ V/rad}\) causes steady-state wander at \(\gamma = 0.9\)).
